      const test = require('node:test');
      const assert = require('node:assert/strict');
      
      const { __test } = require('../server/index.cjs');
      
      test('agent conversation context keeps newest turns within the byte budget', () => {
        const messages = [
          { role: 'user', content: `old request ${'a'.repeat(20_000)}` },
          { role: 'assistant', content: `old answer ${'b'.repeat(2_000)}` },
          { role: 'user', content: `latest request ${'c'.repeat(4_000)}` },
        ];
        const bounded = __test.boundAgentContextMessages(messages);
        assert.equal(bounded.at(-1).content, messages.at(-1).content);
        assert.equal(bounded[0].role, 'user');
        assert.ok(__test.agentContextBytes(bounded) <= __test.CHANNEL_CONTEXT_MAX_BYTES);
        assert.equal(bounded.length, 1);
        assert.equal(bounded[0].content, messages[2].content);
      });
      
      test('a single oversized latest message is explicitly end-truncated on UTF-8 boundaries', () => {
        const content = `BEGIN-${'x'.repeat(40_000)}-${'\u{1F680}'.repeat(8_000)}-END`;
        const bounded = __test.boundAgentContextMessages([{ role: 'user', content }]);
        assert.equal(bounded.length, 1);
        assert.match(bounded[0].content, /^BEGIN-/);
        assert.doesNotMatch(bounded[0].content, /-END$/);
        assert.match(bounded[0].content, /message truncated at the agent context limit/);
        assert.doesNotMatch(bounded[0].content, /\uFFFD/);
        assert.ok(__test.agentContextBytes(bounded) <= __test.CHANNEL_CONTEXT_MAX_BYTES);
      });

I found a concrete stream-handling gap: the built-in adapter accepts EOF as success without requiring a terminal event, and can treat an unfinished tool block as an empty-argument call. I’m testing those cases and checking whether timeout recovery stops the work or only changes its database status.

      function installFetch(responses) {
        const requests = [];

         // already drains, but do it explicitly here too so startup is ordered and

         // a blanket sweep of every 'todo' task with an agent assignee. A blanket sweep
         // would wake every stale assigned task in the workspace on every deploy, which
         // is a token bill nobody asked for.
         const restartedPairs = new Map();

       async function pruneOfflineConnections() {

        // statement below throwing into the catch.
        //
        // mcpAgentPresence is written by touchMcpPresence on every MCP call and read
        // by hasMcpPresence, which compares against MCP_PRESENCE_TTL_MS. That TTL
        // makes a stale entry harmless to READ but does nothing to remove it — there
        // was no delete on this Map anywhere, so every agent id that ever made one MCP
        // call stayed resident for the lifetime of the process. Bounded by the number
        // of distinct agents rather than by traffic, so it is a slow leak rather than
        // a runaway one, but it is one that only ever grows and it already has the
        // sweep it needs sitting right here.
        //
        // Expire on the same TTL the reader uses: anything hasMcpPresence would call
        // absent is exactly what there is no reason to keep.

         if (seenAt < presenceCutoff) mcpAgentPresence.delete(agentId);

         // best effort

      test('resolveHttpBackendBase rewrites Vite loopback to :3142', () => {
        assert.equal(resolveHttpBackendBase('http://127.0.0.1:5173'), 'http://127.0.0.1:3142');
        assert.equal(resolveHttpBackendBase('http://localhost:5173/'), 'http://127.0.0.1:3142');
        assert.equal(resolveHttpBackendBase('https://agensis-backend.fly.dev'), 'https://agensis-backend.fly.dev');
        assert.equal(resolveHttpBackendBase('http://127.0.0.1:3142'), 'http://127.0.0.1:3142');
        assert.equal(resolveHttpBackendBase(''), 'http://127.0.0.1:3142');
      });

        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime('claude'), 'claude');
        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime('Codex'), 'codex');
        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime('AMP'), 'amp');
        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime('grok'), '');
        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime('hermes'), '');
        assert.equal(normalizeRuntime(''), '');
      });
      
      test('listRuntimes reports full desktop catalog shapes', () => {
        const listed = supervisor.listRuntimes();
        assert.ok(listed.daemon);
        assert.ok(Array.isArray(listed.runtimes));
        const ids = listed.runtimes.map((r) => r.id);
        for (const need of ['claude', 'codex', 'amp', 'grok', 'hermes', 'omp', 'goose', 'cursor', 'opencode', 'kimi', 'openclaw']) {
          assert.ok(ids.includes(need), `missing runtime ${need}`);
        }
        for (const r of listed.runtimes) {
          assert.equal(typeof r.label, 'string');
          assert.equal(typeof r.available, 'boolean');
          assert.equal(typeof r.mode, 'string');
          assert.ok(['sdk', 'app-server', 'amp', 'acp', 'cli'].includes(r.mode), r.mode);
        }
      });

        const { buildConnectFlags } = require('../electron/local-runtime/runtimeCatalog.cjs');
      
        const claude = buildConnectFlags('claude');
        assert.ok(claude.args.includes('--no-acp'));
        assert.ok(claude.args.includes('--runtime'));
        assert.equal(claude.env.AGENSIS_ACP, '0');
        assert.equal(claude.classicRuntime, 'claude');
      
        const codex = buildConnectFlags('codex');
        assert.ok(codex.args.includes('--no-acp'));
        assert.deepEqual(
          codex.args.slice(codex.args.indexOf('--runtime'), codex.args.indexOf('--runtime') + 2),
          ['--runtime', 'codex'],
        );
      
        const hermes = buildConnectFlags('hermes');
        assert.ok(!hermes.args.includes('--no-acp'));
        assert.ok(hermes.args.includes('--acp-harness'));
        assert.equal(hermes.env.AGENSIS_ACP, '1');
        assert.equal(hermes.acpHarness, 'hermes');
      
        const grok = buildConnectFlags('grok');
        assert.equal(grok.acpHarness, 'grok');
        assert.equal(grok.env.AGENSIS_ACP_HARNESS, 'grok');
      
        const pi = buildConnectFlags('pi'); // alias → omp
        assert.equal(pi.def.id, 'omp');
        assert.ok(pi.args.includes('--coding-cmd'));
        assert.ok(pi.args.includes('omp'));
      });
      
      test('pickRuntimeId accepts harness ids and pi alias', () => {
        assert.equal(supervisor.pickRuntimeId({ runtime: 'hermes' }), 'hermes');
        assert.equal(supervisor.pickRuntimeId({ harnessId: 'grok' }), 'grok');
        assert.equal(supervisor.pickRuntimeId({ runtime: 'pi' }), 'omp');
        assert.equal(supervisor.pickRuntimeId({}), 'claude');

      test('desktop supervisor binds every child to AGENSIS_SUPERVISOR_PID', () => {
        // Orphaned connect processes (PPID 1 after Electron force-quit) were the
        // root of the "connection dropped mid-turn" melt: nobody read their pipes,
        // uncaught handlers stormed at 100% CPU, and codex app-server could not
        // handshake. The CLI watches this env var and exits when desktop dies.
        const body = fs.readFileSync(
          path.join(__dirname, '../electron/local-runtime/supervisor.cjs'),
          'utf8',
        );
        assert.match(body, /AGENSIS_SUPERVISOR_PID:\s*String\(process\.pid\)/);
        assert.match(body, /detached:\s*false/);
      });

      # Fly.io config for the agensis realtime backend (server/index.cjs).
      #
      # Netlify can't host WebSockets, so the WS realtime + agent-daemon endpoint
      # (/backend/ws) and the rest of the Express API run here. The static frontend
      # stays on Netlify; daemons are pointed here via AGENSIS_DAEMON_BASE_URL.
      #
      # First deploy:
      #   flyctl auth login
      #   fly launch --no-deploy --copy-config --name agensis-backend   # or: fly apps create agensis-backend
      #   fly secrets set DATABASE_URL='...' ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='...' AGENSIS_AUTH_SECRET='...'
      #   fly deploy
      # Secrets live in `fly secrets`, NEVER in this file.
      
      app = "agensis-backend"
      primary_region = "fra"
      
      [build]
        dockerfile = "Dockerfile.fly"
      
      # Fly's default is 5s from SIGTERM to SIGKILL. The backend now drains its
      # WebSockets on SIGTERM (see startBackendServer's `shutdown`), telling every
      # daemon and browser to reconnect with a 1012 instead of dropping them into a
      # reasonless 1006. That drain is bounded by AGENSIS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_MS (3s), so
      # give the machine a little more than that before it is killed — otherwise the
      # SIGKILL lands mid-drain and the close frames never leave.
      kill_timeout = "10s"
      
      [env]
        HOST = "0.0.0.0"
        API_PORT = "8080"
        NODE_ENV = "production"
        AGENSIS_APP_URL = "https://agensis.io"
        # Persistent upload root on the mounted volume (H6). Volume provisioned:
        #   fly volumes create agensis_uploads --region fra --size 3 --app agensis-backend
        # Note: a single volume attaches to ONE machine — durable but not shared across
        # machines; multi-machine scale-out needs object storage (S3/R2).
        AGENSIS_UPLOAD_ROOT = "/data/uploads"
      
      [[mounts]]
        source = "agensis_uploads"
        destination = "/data"
      
      [http_service]
        internal_port = 8080
        force_https = true
        # Keep one machine warm so open WebSockets (browser realtime + agent daemons)
        # are not torn down by idle auto-stop.
        auto_stop_machines = "stop"
        auto_start_machines = true
        min_machines_running = 1
      
        [[http_service.checks]]
          interval = "15s"
          timeout = "5s"
          grace_period = "20s"
          method = "GET"
          path = "/backend/health"
      
      [[vm]]
        size = "shared-cpu-2x"
        memory = "2gb"

      # AGENTS.md
      
      This repository is the open-source Agensis host agent. It does not contain the
      Agensis website, backend, database, or desktop application.
      
      ## Layout
      
      - `packages/agensis-cli/src` is the readable source of truth.
      - `packages/agensis-cli/src/mesh.mjs` owns the agent-mesh listener.
      - `packages/agensis-agent` builds the published single-file npm bundle.
      - `tests` contains Node and Vitest coverage for the daemon.
      - `docs/reviews/` holds dated review and survey documents; `plan.md` is the live implementation plan.
      - `docs/cli-discovery.md` describes how coding CLIs are found on PATH+tool
        prefixes and advertised in capability sync (ACP harnesses including Fx).
      
      ## Versioning
      
      Keep these values identical for every release:
      
      1. root `package.json` version
      2. both package versions
      3. `AGENSIS_CLI_VERSION` in `packages/agensis-cli/src/agensis.mjs`
      4. `SOURCE_VERSION` in `packages/agensis-agent/build.mjs`
      5. generated lockfile package versions
      
      ## Self-update + rollback (`agensis supervise`)
      
      Optional: run `agensis supervise [--profile <name>]` instead of `agensis connect`
      to let an agent trigger an update+reload of its own daemon connection, with
      automatic rollback if the new version doesn't come up healthy.
      
      - **Trigger**: the agent (or anything with --add-dir access to its own state
        dir) writes `~/.agensis/<workspace>/<agent>/update-request.json`
        (`{"targetVersion": "0.1.31"}`) — see `writeUpdateRequest` in
        `packages/agensis-cli/src/state.mjs`. No new network surface.
      - **Install layout**: versions live side-by-side under
        `~/.agensis/versions/<version>/` (each an independent
        `npm install --prefix`), with `~/.agensis/versions/current` a symlink to the
        one actually running. Rollback is a symlink flip + relaunch, never a second
        install, so a broken new version can never block recovering the last-known-
        good one — see `packages/agensis-cli/src/selfUpdate.mjs`.
      - **Health check**: "registered + heartbeating" (a fresh, connected
        `heartbeat.json` from the new process's pid), not "claimed a job" — an idle
        agent with no queued work would never pass a job-claim bar.
      - **State**: `~/.agensis/<workspace>/<agent>/update.json` records
        `currentVersion`/`previousVersion`/`lastAttempt` (daemon/supervisor-owned;
        see `packages/agensis-cli/src/supervise.mjs`).
      - **Surviving a killed supervisor**: `agensis supervise` is a separate process
        from the daemon it spawns, deliberately dumb and stable, so it keeps running
        across daemon crashes/updates. `agensis service install --profile <name>`
        installs it under a macOS user LaunchAgent (`KeepAlive`) or Linux systemd user
        unit (`Restart=always`), so the OS brings it back if it is killed. The service
        file contains no token/workspace data; it selects the existing mode-0600
        daemon profile by name. On restart, supervise re-derives everything from disk
        (no in-memory state to lose).
      - Scoped to host daemons for now — `run_mode: 'sandbox'` (e2b) jobs run in an
        ephemeral VM with no persistent installed daemon to update in this sense.
      
      ## Agent mesh (`--lan`)
      
      Two opt-ins, deliberately separate: `--lan` binds the listener, `--lan-accept-jobs`
      (default off) allows peer-supplied jobs to execute. Do not collapse them into one
      flag. A peer payload picks its own `permission_mode`, `cwd` and `run_mode` —
      including `sandbox`, which spends this host's `E2B_API_KEY` / `GIT_TOKEN` — and
      nothing binds those choices to the hub's ticket, so accepting a connection must not
      imply accepting arbitrary work.
      
      Invariants pinned by `tests/agent-mesh-peer-handoff.test.mjs`:
      
      - one ticket buys one job, then the socket closes
      - `agent_reach_disable` terminates connected peers and clears resident grants
      - a peer job's result rides the LIVE hub socket, and is parked and re-sent if that
        socket is down when the turn ends
      
      **`ws` ESM trap.** These are ESM modules, and `ws`'s ESM default export is the bare
      `WebSocket` class with no `.Server` property — `Server` is attached only on the
      CommonJS entry. Import `{ WebSocketServer }` by name. `new WebSocket.Server()` type-
      checks fine and throws a `TypeError` at runtime; because that throw happened inside
      the `agent_registered` handler, the process guard swallowed it and the rest of
      registration (capabilities sync, ACP prewarm) was silently skipped, so the daemon
      looked healthy while its listener had never bound.
      
      ## Verification
      
      Run `npm run verify`. Do not publish unless it passes and the generated bundle
      reports the intended version through `node packages/agensis-agent/bin/agensis.mjs --version`.
      
      `npm test` runs daemon-spawning suites at concurrency 2 via `scripts/run-tests.mjs`;
      add a new daemon-spawning suite to `DAEMON_SUITES` there.
      
      The mesh and reconnect suites spawn real daemons against a fake hub and redirect
      `HOME` to a temp directory. Keep that redirect in any new test that starts a daemon:
      the startup health sweep kills daemons whose heartbeat looks stale, so without it a
      test run can SIGTERM a developer's live agents. Timing-sensitive paths — a turn that
      has to finish inside the reconnect gap — need margin against the 2s reconnect floor,
      or they pass in isolation and fail under load.
      
      ## Release
      
      Push a matching `agent-v<version>` tag. The publish workflow verifies the tag,
      builds and packs the bundle, and publishes `@agensis/agensis-agent` through the
      npm trusted-publisher binding for `jasonkneen/agensis-agent` and
      `.github/workflows/publish-agent.yml`. It uses GitHub OIDC and has no long-lived
      npm token secret.

      // Per-agent work queue + cancel/dedupe intent helpers. Pure + dependency-free
      // so it stands alone and is unit-testable. (Mirror of scripts/lib/queue.mjs —
      // keep the two equivalent.)
      //
      // Why: the poll loop used to `await` each multi-minute run inline, so the daemon
      // stopped fetching while it worked — rapid mentions from several people queued up
      // invisibly (or were dropped), and there was no way to interrupt. This queue lets
      // the loop keep polling: it enqueues work, the queue runs it one at a time, and a
      // plain-text "stop" picked up on the same poll can cancel the active run.
      
      /** Normalize task text for dedupe: lowercase, strip @mentions, collapse space. */
      export function normalizeTask(text) {
        return String(text || "")
          .toLowerCase()
          .replace(/@[a-z0-9-]+/g, " ")
          .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
          .trim();
      }
      
      /** Burst-dedupe key: same requester + same thread (or channel) + same normalized
       *  ask. A burst of identical pings from ONE person collapses to one job (one ask
       *  never spawns N branches), but two different people asking the same thing stay
       *  distinct. `author` is a display name (not a stable id), so same-named users can
       *  still collide — acceptable until the mention payload carries a user id. */
      export function dedupeKey(message, channelId) {
        const scope = (message && message.parentId) || channelId || "";
        const who = (message && message.author) || "";
        return `${scope}::${who}::${normalizeTask(message && message.body)}`;
      }

      //

      // runtime has said nothing for a while. The pooled Claude SDK and Codex lanes
      // carry their own (tested, subtle) implementations; this helper is for the ACP,
      // direct and sandbox lanes, which previously had none.
      //
      // Pure: no I/O. The caller cancels the underlying work in `onTimeout`; this
      // helper then waits at most `settleMs` for that work to settle so a session can
      // be reused or disposed knowingly, and returns which deadline fired.
      
      /**
       * @template T
       * @param {(ctx: { touch: () => void }) => Promise<T>} run
       * @param {{ timeoutMs?: number, idleTimeoutMs?: number, onTimeout?: (kind: 'hard_timeout'|'idle_timeout') => void, settleMs?: number }} [opts]
       * @returns {Promise<{ result: T | null, timedOut: 'hard_timeout' | 'idle_timeout' | null }>}
       */
      export function withDeadlines(run, { timeoutMs = 0, idleTimeoutMs = 0, onTimeout = () => {}, settleMs = 5_000 } = {}) {
        let hardTimer = null;
        let idleTimer = null;
        let timedOut = null;
        let resolveTimeout = () => {};
        const timeoutPromise = new Promise((resolve) => { resolveTimeout = resolve; });
      
        const fire = (kind) => {
          if (timedOut) return;
          timedOut = kind;
          try { onTimeout(kind); } catch { /* the caller's cancel must never break the race */ }
          resolveTimeout(kind);
        };
        const armIdle = () => {
          if (!(idleTimeoutMs > 0)) return;
          if (idleTimer) clearTimeout(idleTimer);
          idleTimer = setTimeout(() => fire("idle_timeout"), idleTimeoutMs);
          idleTimer.unref?.();
        };
        if (timeoutMs > 0) {
          hardTimer = setTimeout(() => fire("hard_timeout"), timeoutMs);
          hardTimer.unref?.();
        }
        armIdle();
      
        const touch = () => { if (!timedOut) armIdle(); };
        const clear = () => {
          if (hardTimer) clearTimeout(hardTimer);
          if (idleTimer) clearTimeout(idleTimer);
        };
      
        const work = Promise.resolve().then(() => run({ touch }));

        // rejected — the timeout classification must win. The caller's `onTimeout`
        // cancellation routinely settles the pending work itself (resolving a
        // stand-in value, or rejecting because a killed process / cancelled RPC
        // throws), and either shape must come back as `hard_timeout` / `idle_timeout`,
        // never leak through as `run`'s result or a thrown cancellation error.

        // that resolves; both handlers are attached here so neither settlement of
        // `work` is ever unhandled.
        const settled = work.then(
          (result) => (timedOut ? new Promise(() => {}) : { result, timedOut: null }),
          (err) => { if (timedOut) return new Promise(() => {}); throw err; },

        const expired = timeoutPromise.then(async (kind) => {
          await Promise.race([
            work.catch(() => {}),
            new Promise((resolve) => { const t = setTimeout(resolve, settleMs); t.unref?.(); }),

          return { result: null, timedOut: kind };

      //
      // Which warm session a conversation gets to run on.
      //

      // every job is handed the SAME sessionKey — `${workspaceId}:${agent}` — and
      // connectionExecutors.mjs serialises same-key runs behind a keyed mutex. So the
      // queue lets two lanes in and the mutex funnels them onto one connection:
      // effective parallelism is 1. That mutex is CORRECT — two jobs must never race
      // one connection — the missing piece is more than one connection to hand out.
      //
      // A second, quieter consequence: because one session serves the whole silo,
      // consecutive turns in DIFFERENT conversations share one runtime conversation
      // history. A turn in #build is visible to the next turn in a DM. Within one
      // workspace and one agent that is not a privilege escalation, but it is
      // cross-channel bleed nobody chose, and giving each lane its own slot fixes it
      // as a side effect — which also makes it a BEHAVIOUR change, hence the default
      // of 1 slot (exactly today) until someone opts in.
      //

      // path is unit-testable without a subprocess. In Rust a slot would be an owned
      // value the compiler reclaims; here a claim without a matching release is a
      // permanent capacity loss that nothing will catch for us, so `release` MUST be
      // called from a `finally`.
      
      /**
       * @param {{ slots?: number }} [opts] slots per silo; 1 reproduces today exactly.

      export function createSessionSlots({ slots = 1 } = {}) {

        let seq = 0;
      
        const siloState = (silo) => {
          let state = silos.get(silo);
          if (!state) {

            silos.set(silo, state);
          }
          return state;

         * keeps its own warm session (and its own history) turn after turn instead of
         * being reshuffled onto whichever slot happens to be free.

         * ALWAYS returns a slot in [0, size) — never null, and this is load-bearing
         * twice over:

        const claim = (silo, lane) => {
          const state = siloState(silo);

          const sticky = state.byLane.get(laneKey);
          if (sticky !== undefined && !state.busy.has(sticky)) {
            state.busy.add(sticky);
            state.lastUsed.set(sticky, (seq += 1));
            return sticky;
          }
      
          // A slot nobody has bound yet is always better than evicting someone.
          for (let slot = 0; slot < size; slot += 1) {

            const bound = [...state.byLane.values()].includes(slot);

          // move its lane off it — LRU because the lane that has gone longest without
          // a turn is the one whose warm history is least likely to be wanted next.
          //
          // Idle slots are preferred over busy ones, but a busy slot IS eligible: see
          // the contract above. Landing on one means this job queues behind the other
          // on that session's mutex, which is precisely what every job does today.
          let victim = null;
          const better = (a, b) => {
            if (b === null) return true;

            const bBusy = state.busy.has(b);
            if (aBusy !== bBusy) return !aBusy;
            return (state.lastUsed.get(a) || 0) < (state.lastUsed.get(b) || 0);

            if (slot === victim) state.byLane.delete(otherLane);

          state.busy.add(victim);
          state.lastUsed.set(victim, (seq += 1));

      async function runAgentJob(config, job, { signal, requestPermission = null }) {
        const started = Date.now();
        log(`Starting job ${job.id}`);
        const jobRuntime = executionRuntimeForJob(config, job);
        if (config.runtimeLocked && jobRuntime !== config.runtime) {
          const error = `Executor runtime ${config.runtime} cannot accept job runtime ${jobRuntime}.`;
          send(job.ws, {
            action: "agent_job_result",
            jobId: job.id,
            response: "",
            error,
            errorCode: "runtime_mismatch",
            elapsedMs: Date.now() - started,
            metadata: { executionRuntime: config.runtime },
          });
          log(`Job ${job.id} refused: runtime mismatch (${config.runtime} != ${jobRuntime})`);
          return;
        }
        if (isAmpJob(job)) {
          await runAmpAgentJob(config, job, { signal, started });
          if (config.once) {
            log("One-shot Amp job complete; exiting.");
            setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 150);
          }
          return;
        }
        const cursorBuddyIntent = parseCursorBuddyControlIntent(job.prompt);
        if (cursorBuddyIntent && canHandleCursorBuddyControlJobs(config)) {
          await runCursorBuddyControlJob(config, job, cursorBuddyIntent, started);
          if (config.once) {
            log("One-shot CursorBuddy control job complete; exiting.");
            setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 150);
          }
          return;
        }
        const command = buildAgentCommand(config, job);
        const prompt = await buildPrompt(config, job);
        let fullContent = "";
        let latest = "";
        let lastDeltaAt = 0;
        const sendDelta = (content = "") => {
          if (shouldDeferDelta(job.ws)) return;
          send(job.ws, {
            action: "agent_job_delta",
            jobId: job.id,
            content,
            elapsedMs: Date.now() - started,
            model: command.model,
            permissionMode: command.permissionMode,
            permissionFlags: command.permissionFlags,
          });
        };
      
        // One message per tool round trip, so a tool-only turn is visible as it
        // happens instead of silently expanding a single "Thinking …" placeholder.
        const sendStep = (step) => {
          send(job.ws, {
            action: "agent_job_step",
            jobId: job.id,
            kind: step.kind,
            name: step.name,
            detail: step.detail,
            elapsedMs: Date.now() - started,
          });
        };
      
        // One message per finished text block, so a turn reads as the steps the agent
        // actually took — text, its tools, the next text — instead of one bubble that
        // keeps growing with five thoughts run together and no place to interrupt.
        const sendSegment = (segment) => {
          send(job.ws, {
            action: "agent_job_segment",
            jobId: job.id,

            elapsedMs: Date.now() - started,

        sendDelta("");
        const progressTimer = setInterval(() => sendDelta(fullContent), 1000);
        if (progressTimer.unref) progressTimer.unref();

        // exact executable run, so it always gets the unchanged subprocess path.
        const usesBareBinary = !/[\\/]/.test(command.cmd);
        const family = config.fastConnection && usesBareBinary
          ? (isClaudeCommand(command.cmd) ? "claude" : isCodexCommand(command.cmd) ? "codex" : null)

        // once and WHICH one runs cannot be known until the executor reports back —
        // ACP can be declined up front, or bail mid-run and hand the job to the
        // classic CLI. So the parser is always built for a stream-json command, the
        // raw stream is kept alongside it, and each is used only for the format it

        // and skipping the parser on a classic turn dumped raw NDJSON into the chat.
        const parser = command.streamJson

          : null;
        let rawContent = "";
        const executor = createExecutor(job, { family, config });
        // A runtime history belongs to exactly one hub and conversation. Encoding

        const sessionKey = JSON.stringify([config.hubNamespace || "", config.workspace || job.workspaceId || "", config.agent || config.handle || "", laneKeyForJob(job)]);
        const running = executor.run({

          args: [...command.args, prompt],

          // The two deadlines are handed over as a PAIR. timeoutMs caps a turn that is

        // there too rather than leaving the bubble empty until the result frame.

        // numbers, never forward unknown keys. Absent when the runtime had no usage
        // (LocalExecutor, Amp, older SDKs).
        const stopUsage = (() => {
          const raw = stop?.usage;
          if (!raw || typeof raw !== "object") return null;
          const out = {};
          for (const key of [
            "input_tokens",
            "output_tokens",
            "cache_creation_input_tokens",
            "cache_read_input_tokens",
          ]) {
            const n = Number(raw[key]);
            if (Number.isFinite(n) && n > 0) out[key] = Math.round(n);
          }
          return Object.keys(out).length > 0 ? out : null;
        })();
        sendResult(job, {
          action: "agent_job_result",
          jobId: job.id,
          response,
          error,
          ...(stop ? {
            stopReason: stop.reason,
            stopDetail: stop.detail || "",
            numTurns: stop.numTurns || 0,
            // Per-turn spend. Stored server-side, deliberately NOT rendered or
            // broadcast in v1 — agent_jobs.metadata is fanned out to clients.
            costUsd: stop.costUsd || 0,
            permissionDenials: stop.permissionDenials || 0,
            ...(stopUsage ? { usage: stopUsage } : {}),
          } : {}),
          elapsedMs: Date.now() - started,
          model: command.model,
          permissionMode: command.permissionMode,
          permissionFlags: command.permissionFlags,
        });
        log(`Finished job ${job.id} in ${Math.round((Date.now() - started) / 1000)}s`);
        if (config.once) {
          log("One-shot job complete; exiting.");
          setTimeout(() => process.exit(0), 150);
        }
      }

      name: unslop
      description: Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.

      # Unslop
      
      Edit text to remove AI patterns and add human voice.
      
      ## Process
      
      1. Scan for the patterns below.
      2. Rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
      3. Add soul (see next section).
      4. Self-audit: "What makes this obviously AI generated?" Fix remaining tells.
      
      ## Adding soul
      
      Removing patterns is half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious.
      
      - **Have opinions.** React to facts instead of neutrally listing pros and cons.
      - **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences. Then longer ones that take their time. Mix it up.
      - **Acknowledge complexity.** "Impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "impressive."
      - **Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional.
      - **Let some mess in.** Perfect structure looks machine-made.
      - **Be specific.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am."
      
      ## Patterns to detect and fix
      
      ### Content
      
      1. **Puffery.** "pivotal moment", "testament to", "evolving landscape", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "deeply rooted". Cut puffery, state what happened.
      2. **Name-dropping.** Listing media outlets without context. Pick one, say what was said.
      3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
      4. **Promotional language.** "nestled", "vibrant", "breathtaking", "groundbreaking", "renowned", "stunning", "must-visit". Use neutral descriptions.
      5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
      6. **Formulaic challenges.** "Despite challenges... continues to thrive." Replace with specific facts.
      
      ### Language
      
      7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
      8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Just say "is" or "has".
      9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
      10. **Rule of three.** Forcing ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
      11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
      12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
      
      ### Style
      
      13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). Em dashes are an AI tell, and reaching for parentheses instead just trades one tell for another. If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
      14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example. Not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
      15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
      16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
      17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
      18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
      19. **Curly quotes.** Replace with straight quotes.
      
      ### Communication artifacts
      
      20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
      21. **Cutoff disclaimers.** "While specific details are limited..." Find sources or remove.
      22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
      
      ### Filler
      
      23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". "It is important to note that" gets deleted.
      24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
      25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
      
      ### Jargon
      
      26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate, wedge, vector, locus, vantage, nexus, primitive (as noun), harness (as metaphor), surface (as in "API surface"), bedrock, scaffolding (as metaphor), modality, paradigm, gold-plating, ratchet (as metaphor), evacuate (for moving code), endgame, north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. "Substrate" becomes "base". "Wedge in" becomes "add". "Vector" becomes "way" or "method". "Gold-plating" becomes "more than the job needs". "Ratchet" becomes the mechanism's real name or "a limit that only tightens". "Evacuate" becomes "move out". "Endgame" becomes "the last phase". Pick the concrete word.
      
      ### Plain speech
      
      27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
      28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
      29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
      30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number. "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
      31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" becomes "use", "leverage" becomes "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.

    # Agent harness reliability review
    
    Review mode, 22 September 2026. Nine findings: six P1, three P2. No production files changed.
    
    Reviewed current working files in `agensis` at `efb04c6e` and the adjacent `agensis-agent` source at `a9f7e4a`. Both checkouts had existing changes. Findings describe those working files, not pristine commits or deployed binaries. The generated daemon bundle was already modified and was not assessed as the installed runtime.
    
    Scope: built-in Anthropic tool loop, shared MCP dispatcher, job reservation/finalization/reaping, deferred chat and cadence dispatch, permission decisions, relay reconnect/result delivery, desktop supervisor, native Claude/Codex executors, ACP fallback, direct subprocess and sandbox boundaries. SDK-owned transcript persistence and individual third-party ACP implementations remain outside this source review.
    
    Catalog numbers below refer to the supplied `agent-harness-reliability/references/failure-catalog.md`. They identify failure patterns, not claims that Agensis shares the original incident's implementation.
    
    ## Findings
    
    ### R1. P1: Native fallback can repeat work that already ran
    
    **Invariant:** uncertain side effects must not be replayed. Catalog 1.1, 1.7.
    
    **Where:** `../agensis-agent/packages/agensis-cli/src/executor.mjs:43-69`; SDK terminal errors are forwarded from `connectionExecutors.mjs:479-492`.
    
    `createPrimaryExecutor` chooses fallback solely from an error-message regex. A started SDK/app-server turn that eventually returns an error containing `ENOENT`, `Cannot find module`, or `command not found` causes `localExecutor.run(opts)` to repeat the complete prompt. It also disables the native executor for subsequent jobs. The error can describe a failure during work, rather than failure to launch the runtime. The ACP fallback already distinguishes a started prompt and refuses replay.
    
    **Evidence:** a probe using the real primary dispatcher and labelled executors performed one effect in the pooled executor, returned `command not found after earlier tool completed`, and performed the effect again in the local executor.
    
    **Fix:** carry an explicit execution phase or `promptStarted` flag. Permit fallback only on a typed pre-dispatch availability failure. Treat errors after prompt submission as terminal or outcome-unknown.
    
    **Regression:** make a controlled tool complete, then fail the active native turn with each regex-matching error. Assert one effect, no fallback, and no permanent native-lane demotion. Separately prove missing-binary fallback still works before dispatch.
    
    ### R2. P1: Built-in cut streams and provider error events become successful turns
    
    **Invariant:** classify stream termination and refuse incomplete calls. Catalog 2.1, 2.2.
    
    **Where:** `server/builtin-turn.cjs:1350-1422`, consumed by `runToolUseLoop` at `:237-277`.
    
    The parser drains the body and returns without requiring `message_stop`, tracking `content_block_stop`, or rejecting a provider `error` event. It ignores malformed frames and drops the final buffer. An opened tool block with no argument delta becomes `{}` with no `inputError`; the loop dispatches it. A block with parseable arguments is also eligible before the provider has closed it. No tool or message terminal event is required.
    
    **Evidence:** the actual adapter accepted an empty body and a provider error event; discarded an undelimited final text block; and a stream cut immediately after tool start led the actual loop to execute that tool with `{}`. Invalid nonempty JSON is rejected correctly, but that does not close the empty/open-block case.
    
    **Fix:** implement one stateful SSE termination classifier. Flush a complete final block, reject malformed/incomplete frames and explicit provider errors, require completed tool blocks, and attach preserved partial text to one terminal failure. Validate object arguments at the dispatch boundary too. Add bounded continuation only with a checkpoint that prevents duplicate effects.
    
    **Regression:** empty body, error event, cut before arguments, cut after syntactically valid arguments but before block stop, cut mid-JSON, final SSE block without a blank line, and normal terminal stream. No incomplete tool may execute.
    
    ### R3. P1: Reaping a built-in job does not stop its execution
    
    **Invariant:** durable termination must fence later generation and tools. Catalog 4.3, 7.1, 7.2.
    
    **Where:** `server/agent-jobs.cjs:404-477,550-582`; `server/builtin-turn.cjs:1205-1241,1350`, and its model/tool boundaries at `:237-270`.
    
    The provider deadline covers headers only. `finalizeStuckJob` marks the job errored and releases queued work, but never reaches the built-in AbortController. The running loop checks only its local signal, not durable job status. A stalled response can remain open after the reaper frees its job slot; when it resumes, tools can still run. Built-in content writes also never update `lastContentAt`, so the reaper's ten-minute idle predicate measures their start time even if text is arriving.
    
    **Evidence:** held the real built-in provider boundary, called the actual reaper finalizer against a labelled DB double, verified status `error` with an un-aborted signal, then released a tool response. The tool executed after terminalization.
    
    **Fix:** route termination through an execution owner that aborts the exact job. Fence every post-generation tool dispatch with current durable state or an execution lease. Add a body-idle deadline based on meaningful content and update built-in progress. A different backend process must be able to revoke the owner, not merely update its row.
    
    **Regression:** stalled body after headers; reaper during a provider call; cancellation on another replica; healthy output continuing beyond ten minutes. Assert no post-terminal tools or text writes and no second execution overlapping an unfenced first one.
    
    ### R4. P1: Relay results are forgotten before the server confirms persistence
    
    **Invariant:** transport enqueue is not durable completion. Catalog 1.7, 5.2, 6.3.
    
    **Where:** `../agensis-agent/packages/agensis-cli/src/agensis.mjs:262-278,2458-2470`; `server/realtime.cjs:1022-1024`.
    
    The daemon parks a final result only when the socket already appears closed. `send` returns true immediately after `ws.send`; the normal path retains no result, and reconnect flushing removes a parked result on the same evidence. The server handles the result without a commit acknowledgment. If the connection drops after local send acceptance, or server finalization rejects, the only final frame is gone. Parked results are also memory-only and the 33rd evicts the oldest.
    
    **Evidence:** both protocol ends inspected. No result-ack/retry contract exists on this path. This was not tested through a live TCP fault proxy.
    
    **Fix:** persist a bounded terminal-result outbox by full job id; acknowledge only after the server transaction commits. Replay unacknowledged results after registration and return the same acknowledgment for idempotent duplicate submissions. Overflow must be explicit, not silent eviction.
    
    **Regression:** drop the socket after send accepts but before server receipt, reject the server transaction, lose the commit acknowledgment, and restart the daemon with a pending result. Each case must yield one durable answer with no tool replay.
    
    ### R5. P1: Built-in success commits before its final transcript
    
    **Invariant:** terminal state and required output must settle together. Catalog 1.7.
    
    **Where:** `server/builtin-turn.cjs:943-997,1020-1027`.
    
    The built-in path updates `agent_jobs` to `done` and schedules the next task before writing the final message. If that message write fails, the catch attempts `running -> error`; it matches nothing because the job is already done, and returns without repairing the transcript. The final answer may remain a partial, an unpromoted thread message, or be absent. Restart recovery only scans running jobs. The daemon result path already supports a transaction containing both records.
    
    **Evidence:** actual `runAgentTurn` with a DB double that commits `done` then rejects final-message persistence returned `ok:false` while the durable job remained `done` and the queue drain had already fired.
    
    **Fix:** commit terminal state and the required final message in one transaction. Publish and drain only after commit. On an uncertain commit, read back the exact job and linked output before choosing a recovery action.
    
    **Regression:** fail final message insert/update after generation, fail commit acknowledgment, and delete the placeholder before completion. Assert either both records commit or a retryable finalization failure remains; do not repeat generation.
    
    ### R6. P1: Deferred wake claims delete the only recovery record before dispatch
    
    **Invariant:** durable work is acknowledged after a durable handoff. Catalog 1.3, 1.4, 4.4.
    
    **Where:** `server/task-dispatch.cjs:106-120,156-187`; analogous parked-chat ordering in `server/index.cjs:7520-7572`.
    
    Cadence timers and the reaper use `DELETE ... RETURNING` to claim a wake, then call `continueConversation`. A process death between those steps loses the wake. A thrown dispatch error is logged, but the row has already disappeared. The batch reaper deletes up to 128 rows before dispatching them sequentially, so a crash can lose the unprocessed remainder too. Parked chat also forgets its record before dispatch and only reparks selected return reasons.
    
    **Evidence:** injected failure in the cadence reaper's `continueConversation`; a second sweep had no row to retry. Existing claim tests cover competing consumers, not failure after a successful claim.
    
    **Fix:** claim with an expiring lease and attempts, then acknowledge after durable job creation or a documented terminal no-work decision. Bound retries and retain an inspectable dead-letter outcome. Preserve per-conversation ordering without repeating uncertain tool effects.
    
    **Regression:** crash after claim and before dispatch, throw during dispatch, and kill midway through a claimed batch. Restart must recover only unfinished handoffs within a stated retry ceiling.
    
    ### R7. P2: Recovery swallows failure to write terminal state
    
    **Invariant:** failure to finalize is a distinct outcome. Catalog 1.7.
    
    **Where:** `server/agent-jobs.cjs:404-477,504-516,550-582`.
    
    `finalizeStuckJob` wraps the authoritative terminal write and cosmetic cleanup in one catch that discards every failure. Its callers cannot tell a successful finalization from a rejected DB write. There is no readback for commit-unknown errors. A running job may be retried by the next sweep, but the failure is invisible; a committed terminal row followed by failed message cleanup will no longer be selected.
    
    **Evidence:** a rejected terminal write made the actual finalizer resolve normally. This is not a claim that every transient failure permanently strands a job.
    
    **Fix:** return or throw a typed finalization outcome; log and retry authoritative failures, read back ambiguous commits, and isolate best-effort UI cleanup from durable state changes.
    
    **Regression:** reject the terminal write, commit it while losing the acknowledgment, and reject only transcript cleanup. Assert truthful outcomes and eventual repair without rerunning tools.
    
    ### R8. P2: Desktop shutdown never escalates after a successful SIGTERM send
    
    **Invariant:** bounded shutdown must observe process exit. Catalog 7.1, 8.1.
    
    **Where:** `electron/local-runtime/supervisor.cjs:378-400`.
    
    `stopAll` sends SIGTERM, then checks `!child.killed` before sending SIGKILL. Node's `killed` records that a signal was sent, so it is already true for the child that ignored SIGTERM. The escalation is skipped and the session map is cleared. The separate single-agent `stop` path does not use that same escalation guard.
    
    **Evidence:** executed the real supervisor with a child double that accepts SIGTERM but never exits and a controlled timer. Only SIGTERM was sent. The CLI's supervisor-PID watchdog is a separate safeguard, not proof this shutdown escalation works.
    
    **Fix:** use `exitCode` and `signalCode` or an observed exit event; keep ownership until exit or an explicit shutdown failure. Ensure the grace timer can run during Electron quit.
    
    **Regression:** a child that ignores SIGTERM must receive SIGKILL; a child that exits during grace must not. Include the actual Electron quit lifecycle in runtime acceptance.
    
    ### R9. P2: Exceptional stream termination drops usage already reported
    
    **Invariant:** account for actual wire usage, including failed calls. Catalog 3.1.
    
    **Where:** `server/builtin-turn.cjs:1350-1419`.
    
    The usage recorder runs after the async body loop. If iteration throws or the abort check throws, it is skipped even when `message_start` already supplied billable input/cache counts. The comment promising accounting for cut streams applies only to clean EOF. Normal Anthropic cache/input separation is correct; this finding is about missing records, not double billing.
    
    **Evidence:** body emitted a usage-bearing start event and then threw a socket-reset error. The actual adapter rejected and invoked the recorder zero times.
    
    **Fix:** record the accumulated counts exactly once from a finally path, preserving the primary stream failure and never inventing missing usage.
    
    **Regression:** network reset and user abort after usage, successful completion, and failure before any usage. First three record observed usage once; the last records none.

      ---
      name: agent-harness-reliability
      description: Production-hardening knowledge for agent harnesses, turn loops, tool dispatchers, provider streaming adapters, sub-agent orchestrators, and their queue/state/session layers — distilled from 53 real production failures (crash recovery, dangling tool calls, truncated streams, double-billed cache tokens, phantom context overflow, lock-order deadlocks, poison messages, duplicate hooks, silent child death, span floods, prompt cache misses). Use whenever the user designs, builds, reviews, debugs, or hardens anything that runs an LLM in a loop with tools — "agent runtime", "harness", "turn loop", "orchestrator", "agent framework", MCP host, sub-agent spawner, provider router, streaming adapter — even if they never say "reliability". Also use for symptoms like turns stuck in running, a session failing on every message after a crash, costs ~2x, context overflow not matching real tokens, stop that doesn't stop, agents polling in a loop, or exploding trace volume.
      ---
      
      # Agent harness reliability
      
      53 things that broke in ~4 months of running an agent harness in production,
      turned into invariants, a review checklist, and test shapes. Source: iii's
      open-source `harness` (a durable turn loop over a worker/queue/state engine)
      and linked PRs/issues, with inferred recommendations for unlinked incidents.
      
      Read this file, then load only the reference you need:
      
      - `references/failure-catalog.md` — all 53 failures grouped into 12 areas: symptom → root cause → fix pattern, with links to the PR/issue. Load when the user hits a symptom, or to ground a design decision in a real incident.
      - `references/invariants-checklist.md` — ~70 yes/no checks organized by area (A–M). Load for any review or design task; answer every line.
      - `references/testing-patterns.md` — documented regression tests, diagnostic fault-injection methods, and recommended coverage; not all patterns landed upstream. Load when writing tests or reproducing a bug.
      
      ## Modes
      
      Pick one from the request; state which.
      
      **Design** (user is building/planning a harness, loop, dispatcher, orchestrator, adapter)
      1. Map their components onto the harness anatomy below.
      2. Walk `invariants-checklist.md` sections relevant to those components; turn each *violated* or *not addressed* line into a concrete design requirement in their stack.
      3. Output: a requirements list grouped by area, each with the failure it prevents (catalog number). Terse; no essays.
      
      **Review** (user shares code/PR/architecture)
      1. Identify which areas the code touches (transcript, stream, queue, locks, payloads, reconnect, tokens, sub-agents, telemetry, prompt, policy, deps).
      2. For each touched area, answer the checklist lines: holds / violated (file:line) / n/a.
      3. Output: findings ranked by blast radius (session-poisoning and wedge-through-restart first, then silent data loss, then cost, then cosmetics). Each finding: the invariant, where it breaks, the fix pattern, the test that would have caught it.
      
      **Debug** (user has a symptom)
      1. Match the symptom against the catalog (search by phrase: "stuck in running", "fails after restart", "double billed", "overflow", "stop ignored", "deadlock", "reset loop", "duplicate", "silent", "polling").
      2. State the candidate root causes from the catalog, most likely first, and the *one observation* that discriminates them (e.g. "does a fresh session on the same engine work? → transcript poisoning, not provider").
      3. Propose the fix pattern and the regression test shape.
      
      **Test** (user wants coverage)
      Use `testing-patterns.md`. Prefer fault injection against the real binary with labelled test doubles over unit tests of the happy path.
      
      ## Harness anatomy (vocabulary)
      
      ```
      message in → persist (session store) → assemble context (token budget, compaction)
        → stream completion (provider adapter via router) → validate tool-call args
        → dispatch tools (deny-by-default allow-list, approval hook)
        → append results (capped at capture) → repeat until stop
      Each step: a durable, resumable job on a FIFO-per-session queue with retries + DLQ.
      Sub-agents: spawned children with their own sessions; parent may park on them.
      Engine: live registry of workers/functions/triggers; WebSocket to each worker.
      ```
      
      ## The twelve invariants (memorize these)
      
      1. **Every tool call closes.** A `function_call` in the transcript always gets a `function_result` — after crash, cut stream, abort, or child death — or the session is poisoned forever. Recovery synthesizes a structured error result; it never re-executes.
      2. **A cut stream is an error, never an empty success.** Classify end-of-stream explicitly; refuse `null`/partial/non-object arguments before dispatch on every stop reason; keepalives are not liveness.
      3. **Turns are durable jobs.** FIFO per session, bounded retries, DLQ, bounded restart redelivery. Restored jobs wait for *all* dependencies, not just their own registration.
      4. **Failure to finalize is its own failure.** Never coerce a read/write error into "absent" or "skipped". Confirm a timed-out terminal write by readback. A skipped reply is not proof nothing was written.
      5. **One lock per session, never two.** All record writers go through it; pin the turn id across read+write; release across the generation RPC and re-read abort on re-acquire; lock-free pre-check before any cross-session lock.
      6. **Bound payloads at capture, structurally.** Cap results where they enter (elision marker with size + how to re-call); shorten event JSON structurally when possible, with a marked plain-cut fallback when it cannot fit; know the transport frame limit.
      7. **Reconnect replays registrations first and gives up on poison.** Bindings register once per startup; consumers dedupe by function id; resume skips *all* holders.
      8. **Count only wire tokens; `input` excludes `cache_read`.** Estimate what is sent, not what is stored. Compaction never empties the context. The cacheable prefix is byte-identical every turn. Small results age out too.
      9. **Children fail loudly and inherit settings.** Dead-child notice reaches the spawner even after its turn ended; `max_turns` ≠ `completed`; effort/model/budgets inherit.
      10. **Give agents a wait primitive** or they will poll and `sleep`.
      11. **Telemetry has a budget.** Coalesce deltas; no persisted write per event; no span per token; alert on trace bytes/min.
      12. **Policy lives in the dispatcher, not the prompt.** Deny by default; malformed rules fail closed; self-restart is refused in code; full-id dedupe.
      
      ## Ranking findings
      
      Order by consequence, not by how easy the fix is:
      1. Wedges that survive restart / poison a session (1.1, 1.7, 5.1–5.5, 6.1–6.2)
      2. Silent wrong results (2.1, 2.5, 8.1, 8.3, 11.1, 11.2)
      3. Deadlocks and lost user intent (4.1–4.4)
      4. Money and capacity (3.1, 3.2, 3.7–3.9, 8.4, 9.x, 10.x)
      5. Everything else
      
      ## Style
      
      Terse. Cite catalog numbers instead of re-explaining. Give the fix pattern and the test, not a lecture. When the user's stack differs from iii's (no engine, no queue worker, single process), translate the invariant to their primitives rather than saying it doesn't apply — a single-process loop still needs a closed transcript, capped results, one writer per record, and a real end-of-stream classifier.
      
      ## Provenance

      - Harness source: https://github.com/iii-hq/workers/tree/main/harness
      - Engine: https://iii.dev/docs/install
      - Per-item PR/issue links are in `references/failure-catalog.md`.

      # AGENTS.md
      
      This repository is the open-source Agensis host agent. It does not contain the
      Agensis website, backend, database, or desktop application.
      
      ## Layout
      
      - `packages/agensis-cli/src` is the readable source of truth.
      - `packages/agensis-cli/src/mesh.mjs` owns the agent-mesh listener.
      - `packages/agensis-agent` builds the published single-file npm bundle.
      - `tests` contains Node and Vitest coverage for the daemon.
      - `docs/reviews/` holds dated review and survey documents; `plan.md` is the live implementation plan.
      - `docs/cli-discovery.md` describes how coding CLIs are found on PATH+tool
        prefixes and advertised in capability sync (ACP harnesses including Fx).
      
      ## Versioning
      
      Keep these values identical for every release:
      
      1. root `package.json` version
      2. both package versions
      3. `AGENSIS_CLI_VERSION` in `packages/agensis-cli/src/agensis.mjs`
      4. `SOURCE_VERSION` in `packages/agensis-agent/build.mjs`
      5. generated lockfile package versions
      
      ## Self-update + rollback (`agensis supervise`)
      
      Optional: run `agensis supervise [--profile <name>]` instead of `agensis connect`
      to let an agent trigger an update+reload of its own daemon connection, with
      automatic rollback if the new version doesn't come up healthy.
      
      - **Trigger**: the agent (or anything with --add-dir access to its own state
        dir) writes `~/.agensis/<workspace>/<agent>/update-request.json`
        (`{"targetVersion": "0.1.31"}`) — see `writeUpdateRequest` in
        `packages/agensis-cli/src/state.mjs`. No new network surface.
      - **Install layout**: versions live side-by-side under
        `~/.agensis/versions/<version>/` (each an independent
        `npm install --prefix`), with `~/.agensis/versions/current` a symlink to the
        one actually running. Rollback is a symlink flip + relaunch, never a second
        install, so a broken new version can never block recovering the last-known-
        good one — see `packages/agensis-cli/src/selfUpdate.mjs`.
      - **Health check**: "registered + heartbeating" (a fresh, connected
        `heartbeat.json` from the new process's pid), not "claimed a job" — an idle
        agent with no queued work would never pass a job-claim bar.
      - **State**: `~/.agensis/<workspace>/<agent>/update.json` records
        `currentVersion`/`previousVersion`/`lastAttempt` (daemon/supervisor-owned;
        see `packages/agensis-cli/src/supervise.mjs`).
      - **Surviving a killed supervisor**: `agensis supervise` is a separate process
        from the daemon it spawns, deliberately dumb and stable, so it keeps running
        across daemon crashes/updates. `agensis service install --profile <name>`
        installs it under a macOS user LaunchAgent (`KeepAlive`) or Linux systemd user
        unit (`Restart=always`), so the OS brings it back if it is killed. The service
        file contains no token/workspace data; it selects the existing mode-0600
        daemon profile by name. On restart, supervise re-derives everything from disk
        (no in-memory state to lose).
      - Scoped to host daemons for now — `run_mode: 'sandbox'` (e2b) jobs run in an
        ephemeral VM with no persistent installed daemon to update in this sense.
      
      ## Agent mesh (`--lan`)
      
      Two opt-ins, deliberately separate: `--lan` binds the listener, `--lan-accept-jobs`
      (default off) allows peer-supplied jobs to execute. Do not collapse them into one
      flag. A peer payload picks its own `permission_mode`, `cwd` and `run_mode` —
      including `sandbox`, which spends this host's `E2B_API_KEY` / `GIT_TOKEN` — and
      nothing binds those choices to the hub's ticket, so accepting a connection must not
      imply accepting arbitrary work.
      
      Invariants pinned by `tests/agent-mesh-peer-handoff.test.mjs`:
      
      - one ticket buys one job, then the socket closes
      - `agent_reach_disable` terminates connected peers and clears resident grants
      - a peer job's result rides the LIVE hub socket, and is parked and re-sent if that
        socket is down when the turn ends
      
      **`ws` ESM trap.** These are ESM modules, and `ws`'s ESM default export is the bare
      `WebSocket` class with no `.Server` property — `Server` is attached only on the
      CommonJS entry. Import `{ WebSocketServer }` by name. `new WebSocket.Server()` type-
      checks fine and throws a `TypeError` at runtime; because that throw happened inside
      the `agent_registered` handler, the process guard swallowed it and the rest of
      registration (capabilities sync, ACP prewarm) was silently skipped, so the daemon
      looked healthy while its listener had never bound.
      
      ## Verification
      
      Run `npm run verify`. Do not publish unless it passes and the generated bundle
      reports the intended version through `node packages/agensis-agent/bin/agensis.mjs --version`.
      
      `npm test` runs daemon-spawning suites at concurrency 2 via `scripts/run-tests.mjs`;
      add a new daemon-spawning suite to `DAEMON_SUITES` there.
      
      The mesh and reconnect suites spawn real daemons against a fake hub and redirect
      `HOME` to a temp directory. Keep that redirect in any new test that starts a daemon:
      the startup health sweep kills daemons whose heartbeat looks stale, so without it a
      test run can SIGTERM a developer's live agents. Timing-sensitive paths — a turn that
      has to finish inside the reconnect gap — need margin against the 2s reconnect floor,
      or they pass in isolation and fail under load.
      
      ## Release
      
      Push a matching `agent-v<version>` tag. The publish workflow verifies the tag,
      builds and packs the bundle, and publishes `@agensis/agensis-agent` through the
      npm trusted-publisher binding for `jasonkneen/agensis-agent` and
      `.github/workflows/publish-agent.yml`. It uses GitHub OIDC and has no long-lived
      npm token secret.

        }
        for (const row of rows) {
         // This process won the claim. Cancel its timer and dispatch the claimed
         // row now; skipping a claimed local row would lose the wake entirely.

         cadenceWrites.delete(row.lock_key);

           threadParentId: row.thread_parent_id,
          });
         } catch (error) {
          console.error('continueConversation (cadence reaper) failed', error);
         }
        }
        return rows.length;

      function stopAll() {
        const ids = [...sessions.keys()];
        for (const id of ids) {
          const session = sessions.get(id);
          if (!session?.child) continue;
          session.stopping = true;
          const child = session.child;
          try {
            child.kill('SIGTERM');
          } catch {
            // ignore
          }
          // Escalate after a short grace. before-quit is sync and must not block
          // the app forever, so we fire-and-forget SIGKILL rather than await exit.
          setTimeout(() => {
            try {
              if (child.exitCode === null && !child.killed) child.kill('SIGKILL');
            } catch {
              // ignore
            }
          }, 2500).unref?.();
        }
        sessions.clear();
      }

      async function stop(agentId) {
        const id = String(agentId || '').trim();
        const session = sessions.get(id);
        if (!session) return { stopped: false, agentId: id };
      
        session.stopping = true;
        const child = session.child;
        if (child && child.exitCode === null && !child.killed) {
          try {
            child.kill('SIGTERM');
          } catch {
            // ignore
          }
          await new Promise((resolve) => {
            const timer = setTimeout(() => {
              try {
                if (child.exitCode === null) child.kill('SIGKILL');
              } catch {
                // ignore
              }
              resolve();
            }, 4000);
            child.once('exit', () => {
              clearTimeout(timer);
              resolve();
            });
          });
        }
        sessions.delete(id);
        console.log(`[desktop-local] stop agent=${id}`);
        return { stopped: true, agentId: id };
      }

    'use strict';
    
    // A lost COMMIT reply is not proof of rollback. Read the exact job once; a
    // terminal state reached by this transaction also proves its transcript wrote.
    async function commitJobOutcome(db, expected, work) {
     let completed = false;
     let result;
     try {
      return await db.begin(async tx => {
       result = await work(tx);
       completed = true;
       return result;
      });
     } catch (cause) {
      let current;
      try {
       [current] = await db.unsafe('select * from agent_jobs where id = $1 limit 1', [expected.id]);
      } catch { /* outcome remains unknown; never infer rollback */ }
      if (completed && current?.status === expected.status
          && String(current[expected.field] ?? '') === String(expected.value ?? '')) return result;
      const error = new Error(`Agent job finalization failed for ${expected.id}`, { cause });
      error.code = 'agent_job_finalization_failed';
      error.jobId = expected.id;
      error.outcome = current ? 'not_committed' : 'unknown';
      throw error;
     }
    }
    
    module.exports = { commitJobOutcome };

      // SM-5 contract test (docs/queue-plumbing-audit-2026-09-21.md):
      //
      //   "scheduleCadenceWake stores a setTimeout in a Map with no DB shadow. On
      //    multi-replica deploys, a message on replica B can never trigger a wake
      //    scheduled on replica A, and any replica restart loses every scheduled
      //    wake with no recovery. The social-channel continues path sets a single
      //    wake per channel+agent; on a multi-replica deploy, this is race-prone."
      //
      // The fix wires cadence wakes through a durable `pending_cadence_wakes`
      // table that exists in all three schema-sync places (runtime bootstrap,
      // canonical schema, migration), and adds a reaper that recovers rows the
      // in-process timer can no longer fire (lost on restart, lost on a different
      // replica).
      //
      // Properties pinned here:
      //   1. The table exists in the migration, the canonical neon-schema.sql,
      //      AND the runtime bootstrap CREATE TABLE block. Missing any one drifts
      //      a fresh DB. (See AGENTS.md "Schema changes: update THREE places".)
      //   2. scheduleCadenceWake now INSERTs into the table.
      //   3. The timer callback DELETEs the row (with RETURNING) BEFORE firing
      //      continueConversation, so a row that another replica already claimed
      //      does not double-fire.
      //   4. clearCadenceWakes DELETEs the rows in the same call that cancels
      //      the in-process timers — a missed clear cannot leave a stale wake
      //      that re-answers an old message on a timer.
      //   5. The jobReaper interval in index.cjs invokes reapCadenceWakes on every
      //      tick, so an orphan row has at most one tick (30s) of latency.
      //   6. The reaper's DELETE...RETURNING pattern is the atomic primitive that
      //      prevents cross-replica double-fires — only the row that wins the
      //      DELETE gets to fire continueConversation.

    'use strict';
    const { randomUUID } = require('node:crypto');
    
    function createCadenceWakes({ getDb, continueConversation }) {
     const cadenceWakes = new Map();
     const cadenceWrites = new Map();
     const query = (sql, args) => getDb().unsafe(sql, args);
     const leaseMs = 60_000;
     async function dispatch(row) {
      const token = row.claim_token;
      let renewing = false;
      const renewal = setInterval(() => {
       if (renewing) return;
       renewing = true;
       void query(`update pending_cadence_wakes set lease_until = now() + interval '60 seconds'
        where lock_key = $1 and claim_token = $2`, [row.lock_key, token])
        .catch(error => console.error('Cadence lease renewal failed', error))
        .finally(() => { renewing = false; });
      }, leaseMs / 3);
      renewal.unref?.();
      try {
       await continueConversation({ workspaceId: row.workspace_id, sessionId: row.session_id,
        targetAgentId: row.agent_id || null, threadParentId: row.thread_parent_id,
        dispatchWakeId: row.wake_id });
       await query('delete from pending_cadence_wakes where lock_key = $1 and claim_token = $2', [row.lock_key, token]);
      } catch (error) {
       await query(`update pending_cadence_wakes set claim_token = null, lease_until = null,
        next_fire_at = now() + interval '30 seconds', last_error = $3,
        failed_at = case when attempts >= 4 then now() else null end
        where lock_key = $1 and claim_token = $2`, [row.lock_key, token, String(error?.message || error).slice(0, 500)]);
       console.error('Cadence dispatch failed; wake retained', error);
      } finally { clearInterval(renewal); }
     }
     async function reapCadenceWakes({ now = Date.now(), maxBatch = 32, key = null } = {}) {
      const limit = Math.max(1, Math.min(128, Math.trunc(Number(maxBatch) || 32)));
      // Exhaustion after crashes is visible too, even if the catch never ran.
      await query(`update pending_cadence_wakes set failed_at = now(), last_error = coalesce(last_error, 'Dispatch lease expired')
       where attempts >= 4 and failed_at is null and lease_until <= now()`, []);
      const rows = await query(`with due as (
       select lock_key from pending_cadence_wakes
       where next_fire_at <= to_timestamp($1 / 1000.0) and failed_at is null and attempts < 4
        and (lease_until is null or lease_until <= now()) and ($3::text is null or lock_key = $3)
       order by next_fire_at, lock_key limit $2 for update skip locked
      ) update pending_cadence_wakes wake set claim_token = gen_random_uuid(),
        lease_until = now() + interval '60 seconds', attempts = attempts + 1
       from due where wake.lock_key = due.lock_key returning wake.*`, [now, limit, key]);
      for (const row of rows) {
       const timer = cadenceWakes.get(row.lock_key);
       if (timer) clearTimeout(timer);
       cadenceWakes.delete(row.lock_key);
       cadenceWrites.delete(row.lock_key);
       await dispatch(row);
      }
      return rows.length;
     }

      if (cadenceWakes.has(key)) return false;
      const delay = Math.max(0, Math.min(2_147_483_647, Number(delayMs) || 0));
      const wakeId = randomUUID();
      const persisted = Promise.resolve().then(() => query(`insert into pending_cadence_wakes
       (lock_key, workspace_id, session_id, agent_id, thread_parent_id, next_fire_at, wake_id)
       values ($1,$2,$3,$4,$5,$6,$7)
       on conflict (lock_key) do update set next_fire_at = excluded.next_fire_at,
        wake_id = excluded.wake_id, claim_token = null, lease_until = null, attempts = 0,
        failed_at = null, last_error = null
       where pending_cadence_wakes.claim_token is not null`,
       [key, target.workspaceId, target.sessionId, target.targetAgentId || null, target.threadParentId || null,
        new Date(Date.now() + delay).toISOString(), wakeId]));
      cadenceWrites.set(key, persisted);
      void persisted.catch(error => console.error('Cadence persistence failed; local timer will retry', error));
      const timer = setTimeout(() => {

        try {

## Assistant

The server now acknowledges relay results after commit, and the isolated daemon copy retains them on disk until that acknowledgment arrives. Cadence wakes now use renewable leases, bounded retries, and a dispatch identity to prevent a recovered wake from creating the same job twice. The test suites are running while I add the fault regressions.

      // STRANDED "Thinking …" PLACEHOLDERS (2026-07).
